Course 14

Biases and decisions

Why the mind takes shortcuts, the most common biases, how we perceive risk and how to decide a little better.

Lesson 1. Two ways of thinking

1 · Lesson

Daniel Kahneman popularised the distinction between two modes of thinking. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it recognises faces, completes sentences and gives us instant impressions. System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful: it does calculations, compares options and follows rules.

We almost always run on System 1, and it almost always serves us well. But in some situations its shortcuts, heuristics, produce systematic errors we call biases. They are predictable: they recur in most people and under the same circumstances.

The two systems are a useful metaphor, not two separate parts of the brain. The practical point is that intuition is valuable in areas we know well and with reliable feedback, and less reliable in new situations, with numbers or when strong emotions are involved.

2 · Example

A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1 more than the ball. How much is the ball? The answer that jumps out is 10 cents, but it is wrong: it is 5 cents (bat $1.05 + ball $0.05). System 1 proposes; System 2 should check.

3 · Activity

For one day, note one quick decision you made by intuition and one you thought through calmly. In which did you have more prior experience? Which turned out better?
